author: Falyn Stempler
title: All the unanswered questions in Bryan's Kohberger case that may go with him to the grave - NewsBreak
text: Bryan Kohberger was sentenced to life in prison without parole Wednesday after confessing to the murder of four University of Idaho students in 2022. Kohberger, 30, admitted to fatally stabbing four students - Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin at a rental home in Moscow, Idaho, in 2022. He appeared expressionless during his sentencing hearing on Wednesday. When the judge allowed him to speak, he simply replied, "I respectfully decline." However, the victims' loved ones did speak during the emotional court hearing, with many describing the killer as pathetic. Yet, many questions remain unanswered about the tragic case, despite the judge last week lifting a gag order on many documents that were sealed. 1. Motive Though he confessed to committing the crimes, Kohberger repeatedly declined to speak and investigators failed to find a smoking gun connecting Kohberger to the students, according to Moscow police Cpl. Bretty Payne. He also declined interviews with authorities while investigating the case. It remains unclear why he targeted the house and killed the four students. 2. Murder weapon Despite conducting thorough searches, investigators never recovered a murder weapon. Authorities believe he used a knife, though one was never found. 3. Digital footprint Kohberger wiped his electronic devices with software that prevented investigators from digging up any evidence pertaining to the murders, according to Payne. 4. Kohberger's mental state The results of his psychological testing have been sealed. However, Latah County Prosecutor Bill Thompson said his "results of that do not rise to a defense to his conduct under Idaho law." At one point, Kohberger's defense team was reportedly planning to claim disability due to his autism spectrum disorder to avoid the death penalty. 5. Kohberger's background Similarly, there was no evidence presented about his upbringing that could explain how Kohberger could have been "pre-disposed to do the crimes he committed," Thompson said.
